We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies of massive proportions, utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our analysis revealed that roughly 28 percent of 2649 galaxies, selected due to their mass greater than $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ and within a redshift range of 0.05-0.15, exhibited distinct tidal features exceeding one percent flux fraction. Observations indicated an exponential decline in the number of galaxies as tidal features became more pronounced. Additionally, within our defined stellar mass scope, we observed tidal features increase in frequency by two-fold when shifting from $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ to $10^{12}M_{\odot}$. A thorough analysis including pair-counts to estimate the merger rate revealed that within a redshift range of 0.05-0.15 and a 10-year time frame, galaxies of massive proportions experience tidal features resulting from major mergers at a rate of approximately 0.055 year$^{-1}$.

This paper is a component of a research series focusing on the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), a theoretical framework derived from the established equation by Laplace and Poisson. Our findings indicate that, under specific conditions dependent on the object's spin, the ASTG can generate repulsive gravitational fields, noticeably observed in areas surrounding the equatorial plane of the object. As a result, this phenomenon is one of the manifestations of the gravitational radiation forces that occur when a celestial body rotates. Additionally, this effect is one of the first direct evidence of the impact of gravitation on a gravitational field. Our analysis further reveals that, depending on the object's rotational velocity and size, this repulsive force may manifest over vast distances far beyond the object's perimeter, even extending to the surrounding space. Considering these principles, our theory can explain and clarify various previously uninterpreted observations of gravitational phenomena as well as predict future occurrences. Moreover, our findings can potentially reveal new insights into the behavior of gravitating systems including star formation, neutron star and black hole interactions, and young radio sources in distant galaxies. This paper is particularly focused on demonstrating a particular repulsive force arising from the ASTG, an effect not yet reported in literature.

We have gathered a vast dataset containing the optical counterparts of Fast Radio Bursts observed in optical and X-ray spectra. Our findings are based on an extensive collection of 17 detected counterparts, along with 27 reported events from the literature. We considered a range of optical, UV, and X-ray counterparts, along with radio observations of FRBs and their potential optical counterparts. We analyzed the optical flux of FRB 180924, which produced a significant gamma-ray flash but no optical afterglow, consistent with expectations from prompt emission. Moreover, we discussed X-ray, optical, and radio follow-up of FRB 200303, which remains one of the fastest-observed FRB at the time of publication, yielding stringent upper limits to its optical, UV, and X-ray flux. Our upper limits from various optical and UV surveys for FRBs with known radio properties indicate a lower upper limit to their optical flux, which could be due to the FRB's orientation, interstellar medium, or the presence of an accretion disk. Additionally, our upper limits from X-ray surveys reveal that 51% of our sample has a upper limit to their X-ray flux under a blackbody model, which is consistent with the upper limit to their optical and UV flux.

The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to their interconnected linear and nonlinear processes, and the high variability in available modeling frameworks. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. We introduce a modular software model that encompasses various amplifier configurations and nonlinear techniques to provide time and frequency-resolved electromagnetic field data and essential physical properties, enabling characteristics of energy, fluence, and spectral distribution. To showcase its capabilities, we apply our software to the LCLS-II photo-injector laser, an example of a complex CPA-NLO system requiring high power and precise control.

Multimodal language generation capabilities of models like GPT-2 and GPT-3 can be leveraged for producing high-quality text, but it is still uncertain how they can be directed by non-text modalities like images. We propose an innovative method using class labels and detailed visual attributes in an image description task. An image description skill is defined as a sequence of specific visual attributes that capture the essence of a scene, and our approach allows these attributes to be dynamically picked based on an image's visual cues, just like how a painter would approach a piece of art. We test this approach on the image description task where labels are available, and our results confirm that feature engineering plays a crucial role in fine-tuning visio-linguistic models, resulting in better performance and more natural image descriptions, and we also demonstrate how to extend our approach to generate more creative text for complex visual inputs in the form of artist prompts.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through a transaction speed benchmarking process.
Notably, Delegated RingCT transactions can be processed at a faster rate of 5-7 seconds, accompanied by significantly reduced bandwidth, approximately 1 KB per transaction, thereby enabling a higher transaction throughput, estimated at 25-50 transactions per second, due to a joint effort in transaction verification.

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This drawback restricts cooperative learning, since adjusting an existing model to address a new problem can negatively affect performance on earlier tasks handled by other teams. To address this issue, the authors developed a groundbreaking 'continual learning' method and successfully implemented it in solid mechanics for the first time. They utilized recurrent neural networks to predict the behavior of materials undergoing plasticity. Notably, the developed method can be adapted for use in a wide range of network architectures and to predict multiple phenomena. This study's purpose is to stimulate innovative applications of continual learning, facilitating collaborative strategies among the mechanics community in addressing increasingly complex problems. Results demonstrate that the employed method enables the network to continually learn new tasks without trading off previously learned tasks. This study was performed under the aegis of the Mechanics and AI (MechAI) community, a platform promoting interdisciplinary knowledge sharing and collaboration, and its findings reflect the spirit of cooperative learning.

This research examines the decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into a $\Upsilon(nS)$
state accompanied by $\pi^+\pi^-$ particles, where $n=1,2,3$. It's assumed
$\Upsilon(10753)$ belongs to a typical bottomonium under the $4S$-$3D$ mixing
scenario. We find that these specific decay processes have relatively large
branching ratios of $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-3}$ and, notably, align with Belle's
experimental findings, validating our previous assignment of the $\Upsilon(10753)$
bottomonium to the $4S$-$3D$ mixing scheme. Further validation of this work
could be achieved through testing with Belle II experiment data.

This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD to efficiently train deep neural networks with quantized weights. Initially, we transform the quantized neural network training into a sequence of constrained optimization problems that can be iteratively refined. Our method, AskewSGD, is an efficient first-order stochastic approach designed to solve each optimization subproblem. Unlike conventional algorithms, AskewSGD avoids unnecessary activations, in-proGRESS computation, and memory allocation related costs, resulting in a substantial 7-fold speed-up over standard approaches. Additionally, we derive mathematically quantifiable, non-analogous properties of our method that guarantee its convergence to the optimal solution. Our experimental results demonstrate that AskewSGD converges at least three times faster than state-of-the-art methods, such as QNN, with similar accuracy in most cases. AskewSGD's source code is available for open review.

The Continuum Soft Robot project utilizes fully flexible mechanical systems to achieve robust interactions with people and their surroundings, offering excellent interaction capabilities with dynamic and intricate environments. This project is an essential area of study within the emerging field of Continuum Robotics, which poses novel control and estimation challenges. The aim of this research paper is to provide an in-depth analysis of recent control methodologies used in Continuum Soft Robotics, including a detailed examination of their individual advancements and shortcomings. By employing a unified framework that integrates model-based control strategies, this paper ensures comprehensive coverage of existing techniques while offering insightful reflections on potential areas of improvement. Furthermore, the paper identifies key challenges that must be addressed in the near future to establish trust in Continuum Soft Robot systems. The research's primary outcome is the creation of a centralized knowledge base that connects various control methodologies, their associated applications, and corresponding literature.

The Jacobi group $G^J_1(\mathbb{R})$ - specifically its semi-direct product of ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ with $H_1$ - can be embedded into a realisation of ${\rm Sp}(2,\mathbb{R})$ via a 4x4 matrix representation. One-forms and orthogonal dual vector fields are then computed in the S-coordinates for $G^J_1(\mathbb{R})$ to find a metric depending on parameters $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)$. Additionally, metrics on ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ depending on parameters $(\alpha,\beta)$, and in the Siegel-Jacobi upper half-plane, $\mathcal{X}^J_1$, are described in the known balanced Kähler metric depending on parameters $(\alpha,\beta)$. Left-invariant metrics on the manifolds $\mathcal{X}_1\times\mathbb{R}^3$ depending on parameters $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)$ are also determined.

Verifying facts using structured data can be difficult, necessitating a model's
understanding of both language and symbolic computations involving data in
tables. Despite pre-trained language models excelling in confirming simple
assertions, they often falter when handling complex assertions requiring
multiple calculations. In our research, we alleviate this challenge by breaking
down intricate assertions into manageable sub-problems. By employing the
synthesized programs from a weakly-supervised parser, we suggest an innovative
method for generating invalid assertion problems, thereby leveraging the
advantages of soft parsing techniques. We demonstrate the efficacy of our
approach on two prominent fact verification datasets.

The state of the art in learned synthetic image generation involves generative adversarial networks. Initial breakthroughs in the field relied on unsupervised generation, while subsequent advancements, including task-specific supervision, are tied to specific tasks and data sources. Our approach, called latent space conditioning, enables both unsupervised and supervised learning schemes to benefit from a shared latent space, thereby allowing task-independent images to be generated and allowing task-specific supervision to be applied to a shared learning framework. Our low-complexity algorithm capitalizes on the distinct nature of conditional and unsupervised generative adversarial networks to facilitate sharing of latent spaces. Our comprehensive evaluation of the methodology, conducted on a variety of benchmark datasets, demonstrates that LSC produces high-quality, diverse, and varied images. Additionally, our results confirm that the LSC network is capable of generating images that are relevant to the target domain, while also being resilient to adversarial attacks. Our study further reveals that LSC significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of task-specific performance.

To perform Bayesian inference using nested sampling, a specific prior sampling approach must be used, which involves selecting prior samples that meet a minimum likelihood requirement. Two main techniques for achieving this are importance sampling and the step method. The importance sampling approach selects samples from the prior distribution, filtering out those with likelihoods below a specified threshold, whereas the step method moves directly from one sample to another by taking large steps in the parameter space. A specific step method, developed by Sanchez et al., stands out due to its efficient generation of nested samples. Our study involves generating nested samples using various combinations of importance sampling and the step method, before evaluating their statistical efficiency using a simplified template model. By analyzing the impact of different prior settings, we examine the trade-off between computational efficiency and accuracy. Furthermore, we introduce a new method for splitting samples between different threshold values to enhance overall performance.

In fault-tolerant distance labelling, we're tasked with assigning brief descriptions to the points in a network so that knowing any three points' labels allows us to deduce the direct distance between any two of them, excluding the third. Our work proves that any weighted network with a specific layout (or in fact any network with limited complexity) allows the creation of labelled information with a relatively small size, which can handle one failure and predict distances between any two points given the labels of the surrounding points. Building on previous research, our methods improve existing results by offering broader applicability while decreasing information required in some cases and increasing flexibility in other cases.

In this theoretical study, we explore two-particle correlations in time and frequency for a Bose-Hubbard model subject to external driving and dissipation, specifically at and around the point where dissipation triggers a phase transition. We calculate a temporal two-particle correlation function and observe oscillations that decline when the model's real quantum component is present, a behavior that deviates from predictions for traditional Bose-Hubbard models without external driving and dissipation. When the model's real quantum component is absent, however, we observe a specific frequency structure and find that the correlations follow a particular frequency-based pattern, a behavior consistent with a specific light-matter model. We further investigate how the presence of external driving influences this pattern, particularly at the point where dissipation triggers a phase transition, specifically by calculating and analyzing and equal-time two-particle correlation function.

For a given second-order linear elliptic equation with coefficients $A$, $\mathbf{b}$ and a parameter $\lambda$, defined within a bounded $\mathbb{R}^2$ domain $D$ and satisfying specific smoothness and boundedness conditions, we establish existence and uniqueness of the weak solution in $W^{1,p}_0(D)$ for the equation, where $2<p<\infty$, assuming that the equation also includes source and flux terms. Similar results are obtained for the corresponding dual problem under analogous conditions, resulting in the key outcome that the solution's weak derivative is in $L^2(D)$. This study builds upon the study by Lewy and Calderon-Weinberger, which demonstrated the solvability of the equation when the drift term is missing, resulting in a P.D.E. in its weak form. Using the study's findings, we derive the solvability of the equation when the drift term is replaced with a $L^2$-integrable function. Furthermore, we establish the corresponding lower-regularity solvability for the dual problem. Additionally, we study the behavior of the corresponding operator when it belongs to $L^2(D)$, and shows that it can reach the boundary of the domain $D$.

To ensure that medical imaging models produce accurate predictions, it is crucial to implement out-of-distribution detection capabilities. There are doubts whether traditional deep neural network-based methods are effective in identifying shifts in medical imaging domains. In contrast, Gaussian Processes offer a reliable method for distinguishing between in-distribution and out-of-distribution data due to their mathematical nature. Consequently, we suggest an efficient and hierarchical approach to integrate Gaussian Processes within Wasserstein-2 space, which can accurately predict data distributions. By applying these Gaussian Processes to a specific sub-space of the input data, we can achieve significant computational speed-up, making them suitable for real-time out-of-distribution detection. We test the efficacy of our approach by performing experiments on image rotation and medical image segmentation tasks, demonstrating that our method is more reliable than deep neural network-based approaches and equally or even more efficient than a recent Gaussian Processes-based method.

Quantum systems driven periodically experience heat build-up due to resonant excitations, typically leading to a random thermal state. In contrast, a system that is both driven and in contact with a heat bath will instead converge towards a distinct, out-of-balance stable condition. Our study follows the development of an optical-lattice system that is driven and coupled to a heat bath; specifically, we observe the formation of a new form of Bose-Einstein condensation arising from a limited set of anomalous excited states within the system. These special excited states maintain their elevated status despite the drive and heat bath's presence, ultimately giving rise to a unique form of Bose-Einstein condensation. To visually represent these anomalous excited states, we use the analogy of a mountain range, with the system remaining stabilized in these exceptional states, or "peaks", for an extended period. The characteristics of these anomalous excited states can be understood by looking at a contrasting, static scenario featuring a finite-sized system that is in contact with a heat bath.

The article explores the convex solution $u$ of the Monge--Amp\`ere equation in an open convex domain with a nonnegative, bounded right-hand side, along with specific boundary data. A key finding relates Alexandrov's maximum principle, specifically its equivalence to H\"older continuity, for convex functions with zero boundary data. Furthermore, it has been proven that convex $\alpha$-H\"older continuous functions fall into $W^{1,p}$ for $p<1/(1{-}\alpha)$. Crucially, this research establishes the H\"older continuity of the convex solution $u$ under specific boundary data, with sharp bounds for the exponent derived through a method involving a bounding Hessian determinant on an n-dimensional cylinder.

Counting the recurrence of periodic events allows us to measure time. Historically, developing stable and accurate timekeeping devices was a significant undertaking. We will instead examine a different class of timekeeping devices, based on random clicking mechanisms. A comprehensive statistical analysis framework is developed to evaluate the effectiveness of these devices, with a specific example being a single two-level atom driven coherently and monitored via photodetection, representing an extreme instance of a non-repeating clock. Using Quantum Jump Monte Carlo simulations and the photon counting waiting time distribution will independently validate the main findings.

This research centers on Software Defined Networks (SDN) to address the challenges of traffic engineering, fault prevention, and service delivery within reliability and energy constraints. Utilizing Fog computing, we focus on optimizing distributed traffic flows to achieve real-time service delivery, effective failure recovery, and fault avoidance in the context of Service Function Chains (SFCs). To address these issues, we developed an FRFP architecture and two algorithms: the Optimal Fog-Supported Energy-Aware SFC rerouting algorithm (OFES) and the near-optimal Heuristic OFES (HFES). By combining these tools, we optimize energy consumption and network reliability while minimizing Quality of Service constraints and network congestion. Our approach, though tested under real-world conditions, assumes ideal resource availability and perfect network communication, thus allowing for near-optimal traffic distribution and network congestion avoidance. Our findings show that the OFES algorithm achieves an 80.91% reduction in network bandwidth usage, an 82.61% decrease in transmission delay, and $53.21$ kW/h energy savings, comparable to a 201.79% increase in energy savings for the HFES heuristic.

Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered around optimizing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images within the same class, minimizing distance between images in distinct classes. Various forms of pair-wise loss strategies have been proposed. To consolidate this diverse loss landscape, we've developed a distinct method, gradient guidance, to isolate the individual gradients of positive and negative examples to inform parameter updates. Through gradient guidance, we've re-examined a range of loss strategies, revealing their underlying mechanics and identifying key factors that contribute to their effectiveness. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that fusion of complementary loss strategies can lead to improved results, ultimately paving the way for the creation of hybrid learning systems.

In this context, we consider an erasure channel sending quantum information to a receiving party as a series of rectangular slices of a quantum system. A hyper-invariant d-DFT matrix properties inspire an efficient algorithm for computing the quantum entropy of the received information on each slice, with corrections for some previously published mergers algorithms' shortcomings. Our algorithm applies to any d value, with calculations based solely on the eigenvalues of a receiving system sub-hamiltonian and a small prefactor depending on d. Additionally, we propose a novel parent d-DFT matrix merger with corrections for the parental structure previously identified by Borelsky in matrices with x and y divisibility of x+y>1.

Our study of magnetized radio filaments at the center of the galaxy utilizes MeerKAT data by examining the distances between groups of these filaments. A sample of 44 groupings containing 174 radio filaments was studied and their shapes were analyzed. Many grouped filaments were found to resemble harp strings or comets with tapered tails, in contrast to loop-shaped structures. Additionally, we found no loop-like filaments in our sample that exhibited straight or curved arms. We propose that the observed filament configurations may form through the gravitational attraction of pairs or small groups of ionized clouds prior to their advection toward the central black hole. This scenario could also be indicative of the detection of Gravitational Waves in the galaxy center, their effects leading to the observed filament arrangements. We also provide an argument as to why Gravitational Waves, capable of causing the observed filament arrangements, may remain undetected by LIGO.

A proposed paper suggests a new method of distributed leader-follower control for achieving conservation voltage reduction in unbalanced three-phase distribution systems by optimizing DERs through the scheduling of smart inverters. The method considers primary-secondary networks and loads influenced by voltage. The system complexity is minimized through the creation of zones in the network based on connectivity. The large-scale optimization is then reduced to smaller, solvable problems using the bisection method. The method does not require synchronized data and relies on the local exchange of data between adjacent zones. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation using open source tools and real-world data from Clemson Testbed.

We investigate non-stochastic bandits and experts in a delayed context, where delays are contingent upon both the time and arm choice. While delayed settings with time-dependent delays have been thoroughly studied, considering arm-dependent delays is more reflective of real-world applications, but raises additional technical obstacles. In the experts scenario with complete knowledge, we create an algorithm achieving a first-order regret bound, highlighting the relationship between delays and losses. This algorithm also results in a first-order regret bound for bandits, given knowledge of missing losses. These are the first regret bounds established for delayed settings, taking into account the best arm's losses and delays only. When no additional information is provided in the bandit scenario, we modify Zimmert and Seldin's algorithm and prove a regret bound despite limited knowledge. The analyses depend on a new bound on the drift, illustrating an algorithm's improved performance following one round's anticipation.

Current text-generation algorithms in dialogue can be flawed. Specifically, optimizing task success using reinforcement learning alone often leads to low lexical diversity in task-oriented settings. The proposed reason is a lack of fundamental understanding of text-generation objectives and how they impact the learning process during model training. A novel theoretical framework has been developed for generating text in dialogue, surpassing existing theories by allowing analysis of multiple goals inherent to text-generation. The new framework also provides theoretical guarantees for learners who adapt their predictions based on past assessments. The experimental results demonstrate the significance of task-specific objectives in dialogue generation, and the introduced framework facilitates future theoretical research in this area.

Following Quantum Chromodynamics' 1972 formulation, a breakthrough in its regularization came when Kenneth Wilson applied it to Euclidean lattices. This opened doors for in-depth numerical analyses of QCD's non-perturbative features, exemplified in the initial studies by Michael Creutz. Subsequently, investigations into the QCD phase diagram and the thermodynamics of hot, dense strong-interaction matter gained significant momentum. In this concise review, some key outcomes from over four decades of lattice QCD research on QCD thermodynamics are compiled.

A type of Gaussian process regression that accounts for the variability in data
known as heteroscedasticity is used to develop predictive models for the ultimate
loads experienced by ocean-based wind turbines, specifically the torque and base
forces associated with the towers, blades, and foundations. Previous studies have
identified some issues with previous models that accurately simulate statistics from
data related to wind turbine loads - as they sometimes incorrectly predict
statistics when considering changes in wind loads, essentially counting random
fluctuations as actual events. Some surrogates also fail to properly model
correlations among various loads. To address these concerns, a new probabilistic
model is created using a combination of Gaussian processes and is tested with
data related to loads on offshore wind turbines to ensure it accurately estimates
probabilistic outcomes. The model is then used to study the statistical variation
of hub shearing forces and base loads along the turbines' vertical direction and
how this affects the overall power production.

Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis information dissemination. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis communication and management. This research focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, aiming to leverage these insights to infer real-time public opinions. By combining data mining and natural language processing techniques, we examine public sentiment and topic discussions following the earthquake. Our approach utilized LDA for topic modeling and BERT for sentiment analysis. Results show users shared supportive messages and engaged with relief efforts, expressing their desire to have their concerns heard by authorities. The implemented methodology demonstrated success, and future directions for related studies are also outlined.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the quotient $G/\gamma_{c+1}(G)$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. In this work, we establish the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree for Generalized Solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$ and explicitly calculate the Lyndon-Nichols problem for a wide range of Generalized Solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$. Our findings also encompass the classical Solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $BS_n$.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. What's more, this approach effectively considers the continuity of molecular structures and is resilient against noisy data.

This paper presents SceNDD: a novel naturalistic driving dataset derived from
instrumented vehicle data collected in downtown Indianapolis over the course
of 68 driving sessions with various drivers. Each session lasted approximately
20 to 40 minutes. Our primary aim in creating this dataset is to supply the
research community with realistic driving scenarios encompassing diverse
trajectories and driving behaviors. SceNDD features a comprehensive set of data,
including the ego-vehicle's waypoints, velocity, and yaw angle, as well as
instrumented data such as lap-top camera images, and vehicle instrument
cluster data. We have created three distinct ways to utilize this dataset:
(1) naturalistic driving with standard visualization techniques, (2) naturalistic
driving with augmented reality applications, and (3) simulated driving within
3D environments. Additionally, we have provided a starting point for naturalistic
and augmented reality adventures on the SceNDD website. Our 10-minute long
naturalistic driving video is presented at the workshop. Any interested party
can acquire the full dataset at the website indicated in the paper.

In connection with the information paradox problem, theories such as BCFT and ICFT are gaining attention. As a contribution to this area of study, we have developed an approach to reflected entropy in the context of BCFT/ICFT. Starting with BCFT, we define left-right reflected entropy and establish its dual description using AdS/BCFT, specifically through the entanglement wedge cross section area. Additionally, we have worked out how to calculate reflected entropy in ICFT. With these tools, we are able to reveal a universal behavior of the Markov gap in specific situations. Furthermore, our work has helped to clarify the holographic representation of boundary primary correlation functions via this left-right reflected entropy and entanglement wedge cross section duality.

Research on Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) systems has intensified due to their potential for controlling the communication environment and combating multi-path interference effectively. Nonetheless, the precision of channel estimation in such systems is significantly compromised by the increased risk of underutilized cyclic prefix resulting from additional cascaded RIS channels, as well as hardware impairments. This paper introduces an advanced Extreme Learning Machine (ELM)-based method for estimating RIS-assisted OFDM channels with inadequate cyclic prefix and hardware flaws. Initially, a computed input form with a reduced number of variables is created to enhance the learning capacity of ELM structures. Next, a dual-structured ELM (D-ELM) model is developed to optimize the channel estimation by combining two ELM models operating in parallel. Finally, a weighted average operation is applied to produce the ultimate estimated channel. The results from our experiments reveal that the proposed dual-structured ELM channel estimator offers remarkable enhancements over existing methods.

We are investigating a type of equality related to the work exerted on a system being measured and characterized by a single observable, denoted as the SEIF, whose proof relies on a refined form of the fluctuation theorem. When applied to a particular type of measurement, known as non-projective measurement, the SEIF takes on a more substantial significance. A scenario involving a qubit being measured with two possible outcomes - zero or one - serves as an example for further analysis and discussion. Within this context, one can identify a suitable work exerted in relation to measurement, satisfy the SEIF in its original form, and explore the drawing process as it relates to entropy variation. However, upon closer examination, it becomes apparent that drawing or entropy variation cannot be reliably captured through this work exerted in relation to measurement once the system has undergone a measurement. Yet, it's also demonstrated that drawing can be represented by a work exerted in relation to measurement followed by a conditional phase evolution dependent on the measurement record. Furthermore, one can show the SEIF remains valid even if the work exerted in relation to measurement is replaced by a more generalized form of work that's consistent with the principles of non-projective measurement. A simple model - the dimer model, where the system consists of two qubits coupled to a quadruplet superconducting circuit - has been used to verify numerically both the original and generalized forms of the SEIF as well as the influence of various parameters on the S

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions.

The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in widespread losses and economic disruption and remains a top priority for research efforts. As part of the measures to combat it, many contact tracing COVID-19 apps have been developed and are being used globally, especially in Europe. These apps aim to decrease the virus's spread by recommending users to self-isolate when they have interacted with an infected individual. The app's functionality relies on the transmission of user data, including location and identification information, to central servers and to other users. This data exchange has raised significant concerns about user privacy, prompting numerous analyses and research efforts. In this article, we explore the privacy risks associated with these apps, specifically targeting the Brazilian model, which stands out for using a different approach by transmitting Bluetooth interaction data instead of the detailed information transmitted by the European models. We also evaluate recent European apps for consistency with current data protection standards, specifically highlighting the issues with the German, UK, and French models. Furthermore, this article outlines proposed amendments to enforce a recent European Union data protection directive, specifically Article 6, that has implications for the COVID-19 apps. We also present a simple solution to protect user privacy while maintaining the app's functionality, incorporating the use of zero knowledge proofs verification. The proposed solution is implemented in the Coronavirus-SUS model, which achieves a high level of protection for user privacy while maintaining the app's utility.

The central nervous system's underlying physiological processes that drive conscious experiences have long been the focal point of research in cognitive neuroscience. In contrast to classical mechanics, the early 20th century saw the emergence of quantum theories describing the behavior of matter and energy. Notably, these quantum descriptions, although minimally nuanced, hinted at a fundamental shift in our understanding of the world. Subsequent decades saw the development of increasingly refined quantum theses, such as the famous Orch-STR model proposed by Hugh Everett, which used quantum mechanics to explain consciousness, despite significant resistance to its claims. In this piece, we will examine the core arguments and flaws of these theories, before illustrating a potential framework for interpreting the evidence supporting the Orch-STR model, while also addressing its limitations, with the ultimate goal of presenting a more plausible quantum explanation for the complex phenomena observed in human neuroscience.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems.

A cluster of young compact asteroids connected to 39991 Iochroma undergoes a dynamics analysis in this study. Our findings show the Iochroma family's location within two adjacent three-body resonance zones - specifically 3J-1M-3 and 5J 3S-2. This paper establishes the precise positioning of these resonances as well as their demarcation boundary, providing orbital elements approximations that verify a previous study. To gain insight into Iochroma's behavior at the 3J-1M-3 resonance, a formal perturbation theory expression for its location within this zone is derived. Furthermore, an analysis is conducted of a dozen other asteroids within the 39991 family, confirming their association with Iochroma. This leaves just one remaining member of the 39991 family unaccounted for, which is labeled as asteroid X. To correlate the location of Iochmon with its corresponding quasiperiodic frequencies, a combination of the Iochmon's elements and those of its Lagrangian coordinates are analyzed. This is done through the application of the fast Fourier transform on its osculating elements. Our analysis reveals that Iochmon is positioned within the 3J-1M-3 resonance, whereas the resonant family member 21367 was initially thought to be associated with this specific resonance. A subsequent analysis of the Iochmon's dynamics at the 5J 3S-2 resonance however, suggests that this particular resonance

Building upon Ramanujan's well-known formula for odd zeta values, we establish two new expressions using the Hurwitz zeta function. We then create a generating function for a specific series that includes these zeta values, and prove it by employing known results from the theory of modular forms. Furthermore, we validate an accuracy conjecture related to this generating function through a straightforward proof.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that it is isomorphic to the cohomology of a complex elliptic T-complex naturally arising from the Segal space associated with the elliptic cohomology theory itself, segregated from its action on constant functions. This result significantly simplifies a computation previously conducted in [SaZi], which involved T-rational homotopy theory.

Recent uses of machine learning in algebraic geometry and physics are explored,  
revealing how problems in this field can be easily translated into tensor mapping,  
a concept suitable for supervised learning, as well as offering a chance to use unsupervised  
methods to analyze geometrical data. A primary aspect of this project involves understanding  
how to use geometry within machine learning, as well as how artificial intelligence can be applied  
to advance mathematical research. This discussion is reflected through several examples,  
including a geometric analysis of self-similar sets from a recent paper on Lie groups by Daskalakis et al,  
as well as how the theory of Chow quotients can be applied to various tools in machine learning,  
enabling the creation of new instruments. This meeting hopes to foster a discussion between  
mathematicians and physicists on using machine learning, as well as between mathematicians and  
computational experts to better understand how to use geometry, leading to novel outcomes.

This paper provides a comprehensive, next-to-leading-order examination of the angular distributions in $J/\psi$ production through $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta_c, \chi_{cJ}$ ($J=0,1,2$) using the nonrelativistic QCD factorization method (NRQCD). The study derived the numerical expressions for total and differential cross sections, specifically $\frac{d\sigma}{d\cos\theta}=A+B\cos^2\theta$, and included newly-calculated QCD corrections. This analysis led to moderate enhancements of the $\alpha_\theta$ parameter in $J/\psi + \chi_{c0}$ and $J/\psi + \chi_{c1}$ and significant reductions in $J/\psi + \chi_{c2}$ production; the value for $J/\psi + \eta_c$ remained nearly unchanged. Comparing our predictions with experimental results revealed that ${\alpha_\theta}_{J/\psi + \eta_c}$ matched the $\textrm{B}\scriptsize{\textrm{ELLE}}$ measurement, whereas ${\alpha_\theta}_{J/\psi + \chi_{c0}}$ remains incompatible and this discrepancy persists despite attempts to adjust the charm-quark mass, the renormalization scale, and the NRQCD matrix elements.

Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be divided into two categories: those who understand the function of PINs (enthusiasts) and those who do not (casual users). Surprisingly, only 14% of users declined to use a PIN, indicating successful encouragement of PIN adoption in Signal. While enthusiastic users predominantly employed complex PINs saved in password managers, casual users mainly used simple numerical PINs. To strengthen the security of casual users, enhancing awareness about the true purpose of PINs and the features they offer could be beneficial.

This technical note details the development of Gaussian quadrature rules designed to efficiently and precisely evaluate the integrals of products involving the solar irradiance function, as defined by ASTM standards, and user-defined smooth functions. The method's ability to produce accurate results with minimal evaluations is particularly beneficial due to the solar irradiance function's non-smooth, highly oscillatory nature. The accompanying Julia software facilitates the computation of solar-weighted quadrature rules across varying bandwidths or point counts. The described technique is anticipated to significantly aid solar-energy computations, where the user-defined function may involve complex and time-consuming calculations such as absorbance derived from solving Maxwell's equations.

The curvature formed by the Hessian matrix or its generalized Gauss-Newton approximation holds significant value in developing training algorithms for deep networks. However, current methods based on automatic differentiation and Kronecker-factored block diagonal approximations disregard noise in mini-batch datasets. Our new model, ViViT, capitalizes on the low-rank structure of the generalized Gauss-Newton approximation without introducing additional simplifications, enabling efficient computation of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and per-sample directional derivatives. This allows ViViT to achieve a balance between computational cost and accuracy, making it scalable for performance benchmarks, including analyzing the impact of noise on the structural properties of neural network training.

Numerous languages attribute gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. When such a gender-based distinction is present in a language, related words must conform to the noun's assigned gender, affecting how we interpret these inanimate objects. As inanimate objects sharing the same gender draw closer together in word representations, we observe this distinct categorization in these languages. However, conventional debiasing techniques have not proven successful in eradicating this distinction. To rectify this, we discovered that selectively eliminating grammatical gender influences during pre-training can help reduce the spurious gender-based connections. As an example, we enhanced the performance of existing models on synthetic and real-world text tasks by implementing this straightforward solution.

We establish that any nitely generated group displaying both a certain kind of "staircase structure" or "dynamic behavior" is essentially a virtually abelian group or is isomorphic to the projective linear group of a two-dimensional space over a finite field. Additionally, our findings align with established results by Dhruv Murthy and Smith when considering groups that are nitely generated and abelian. Furthermore, our work also provides a broader interpretation and refinement of a previous conjecture proposed by Bubi, Gomez, Kechen Lian, and Winther.

Estimating an object's pose is a crucial aspect of most visual pipelines in robots and 3D vision as a whole. This study tackles the challenge of accurately positioning new objects with no prior knowledge, a problem prevalent in many real-world applications. Many current methods are tied to a vast dataset of viewed objects. This research presents a new approach called Projector-Catcher (PC), an efficient and robust system for 2D and 3D pose estimation that relies on a unique geometric representation. It focuses on new objects with unknown shapes but easily identifiable features like signs, symptoms, or contours. It then uses a projector to cast a cognitive shadow of the object onto a 2D image, followed by a catcher that determines the 3D pose by analyzing the projected shadow and the original 2D image. This study demonstrates PC's robustness, efficiency, and accuracy on a new sign estimation benchmark and compares its performance to other prominent pose estimation models.

Predicting short-term traffic is a widely researched area within intelligent transportation systems. However, existing forecasting systems face significant limitations due to their reliance on real-time data. The 2022 Traffic4cast challenge at NeurIPS addressed this issue by using publicly available sparse data. Our team submitted a solution to the expanded challenge of predicting short-term sparse traffic dynamics. We employed a novel multi-task network approach that incorporated a similarity measure to enhance feature extraction. We also introduced a task-specific association mechanism to improve prediction accuracy. Our results demonstrated the efficacy of our approach in predicting short-term traffic volume and travel time, with our top-ranked performance being maintained in the secondary challenge of predicting short-term traffic density.

This study presents VACA, a new family of variational graph autoencoders developed specifically for causal inference tasks where there are no hidden confounding factors, using solely observational data and causal graphs. VACA models key aspects of a Structural Causal Model (SCM) without requiring any assumptions about its underlying parameters. By leveraging these properties, it provides a versatile framework for simulating hypothetical scenarios and making predictions based on past actions. Our experiments confirm that VACA effectively approximates various interventional and counterfactual scenarios in different SCM setups. Moreover, we apply VACA to assess counterfactual fairness in classification tasks, as well as train fair classifiers that maintain high performance standards.

State-of-the-art radio interferometers such as the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) are now capable of producing massive data at speeds of hundreds of gigabits to terabits per second. This significant data rate complicates radio data analysis and necessitates an expensive post-processing phase. Traditional systems fail to detect numerous transient sources because they rely on a limited range of processing methods. In order to extract the most value from sensitive radio telescopes, advanced systems with fast data processing, real-time analysis, and automated detection algorithms are required. Our team introduced a novel system at the Irish LOFAR station capable of producing oriented images at a rate of one image per five minutes in 2003. The system, called REALtime Transient Acquisition (REALTA), is based on an automated system that integrates data processing, image formation, image detection, and variable time-scale analysis. In this study, REALTA was put into action in three distinct modes: survey, follow-up, and search for specific targets. The transient detection capabilities of REALTA were also evaluated during a 24-hour testing period. The testing outputted intriguing results including known pulsars and possible GRB electors which are discussed further.

In recent years, advancements in machine learning and artificial intelligence have driven significant growth in photonics research, leading to cutting-edge photonic systems including traditional waveguides, nanoantennas, and metasurfaces. The innovative application of AI-driven methodologies empowers the development of smart photonic devices rooted in fundamental light propagation principles. Artificial intelligence and machine learning concepts are now integrated into optical systems to create novel, complex structures beyond conventional optical-assisted transmission media. We are poised at the threshold of an era of intelligent metaphotonics, leveraging AI/ML to explore unconventional light-matter interactions and open up unprecedented avenues for optical manipulation and mediated communication. This review article surveys the current state of metaphotonics powered by machine learning, discussing its underlying principles and recent groundbreaking findings.

The high-risk, high-reward nature of filmmaking means predicting which movies will be profitable at the box office has become a daunting task. In an effort to minimize financial losses and maximize profits, the film industry and academic institutions have devoted significant resources to developing methods for estimating movie revenue. This research delivers a two-pronged contribution: first, a comprehensive dataset containing revenue reports for 1894 films produced between 1990 and 2019 was developed, expanding on a similar dataset from 899 movies, which revealed a strong correlation between generated forecasts and actual revenue; second, a novel machine learning method was explored, which considers the intricate relationship between movie characteristics and revenue, ultimately revealing that the characteristics an movie has can directly influence its projected income.

The energy shift poses a threat to energy system stability, and thus, in this research, we investigate the effect of energy storage devices on system stability in response to non-sinusoidal voltage patterns. Specifically, we analyze the stability of a power grid that utilizes tapless transformers with coupled energy storage units, which react to the phase and magnitude of the dynamic voltage. The success of energy storage units in managing sudden changes depends on their synchronization with the power network, and this synchronization is achieved through an optimal control policy that focuses on correcting deviations in voltage phase and magnitude caused by non-sinusoidal patterns, which are driven by energy production and consumption patterns. The stability of the power network is then determined by finding the size of storage units needed to keep voltage dynamics stable near the equilibrium point, which is established by solving a two-person game between energy production and consumption patterns and energy storage units, and this size is shown to be dependent on tap positions of the transformers.

Cyber Physical Systems are transforming into cohesive units, allowing multiple systems to collaborate in achieving a complex objective, embracing a systems of systems topology. In the robotics field, this trend is evident in the formation of swarms, each consisting of subgroups with distinct capabilities, working together to execute a mission and accomplish a common goal. A key challenge arises from the lack of standardized methods to integrate diverse cyber systems, each equipped with unique processing capabilities, into a unified CPS framework. This paper addresses the aforementioned issues by proposing a modular CPS framework that unifies diverse cyber systems and leverages a novel swarm optimization technique for intelligent decision-making.

Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions display a notable increase in ultraviolet and soft X-ray frequencies, which can be attributed to distinct radiation mechanisms. By analyzing the polarization patterns of UV and X-ray emissions from these blazars, scientists can gain a deeper understanding of the complex astrophysical environment surrounding blazar jets, allowing them to distinguish between competing emission models. This research employs a novel Monte-Carlo code called MAPPIES to simulate polarized scattering signatures associated with a Compton process that might be producing UV and soft X-ray excess in certain blazars. Predictions are made about the polarization characteristics of the scattering process and how they may vary in response to variations in the electron energy distribution. The research estimates that polarized scattering should contribute no more than $5\%$ to the total UV flux.

In our study of complex optimization landscapes, we demonstrate the possibility of achieving their analytic continuation. By applying mathematical principles from harmonic and advanced analysis, we establish that various features of these landscapes, being extremely irregular in a real number system, become regular and conform to principles of analytic continuity in a complex number system. This discovery carries significant implications, allowing us to construct unique solutions to optimization problems over complex landscapes. This innovation sparks new avenues of investigation, including the potential for distinct phases in optimization processes and the occurrence of complex phenomena during transitions between them.

To develop optimal methods for identifying identical pure states with perfect accuracy using limited resources, we investigate effective strategies for analyzing multiple state copies in real-time.  These optimized methods utilize specific measurements, may be adaptive and only use each copy's local properties, resulting in the potential for a more resilient process that can still produce optimal results even with partial data loss.  By highlighting existing research that shows local measurement methods are capable of achieving global optimal results with 6 copies, we focus on developing the most resistant method possible for analyzing a single state.  This optimized method involves taking the median local polymitration of each copy.  Initially, we confirm that it achieves global optimal results with just 5 copies.  Furthermore, we verify that it is particularly resistant to data loss by determining that it remains effective with up to 40% of the data being missing.  Notably, this optimized method involves simpler calculations compared to the original method, especially when dealing with large datasets.  Additionally, we extend our findings to a broader group of identical states by determining that it is possible to identify certain types of states with as few as 3 copies, which is an improvement over previous research requiring 5 copies.  Furthermore, we confirm that this optimized method remains effective in most cases with data loss, with specific exceptions occurring when data loss affects the most measurement-sensitive measurements.

Baryon creation is investigated using a quantized fragmentation model based on QCD strings. Baryons are generated through a process that is straightforward to understand, which involves a QCD string breaking up into causally linked parts. A simplified model, representing a QCD flux tube with properties tied to the mass spectrum of light mesons, can replicate the masses of light baryons.

In the study of the sun's interior using sound waves, the speed of these waves when moving along the same meridian in opposite directions helps scientists understand the movement of the sun's fluid surface horizontally from the north to the south.  Researchers observed that the longitudinal averages of the speed of these waves when moving towards or away from the sun's poles had different patterns depending on whether they looked at active regions or the surrounding areas.  The study found the difference in the speed of these waves when related to a specific measure of solar activity was significantly higher when based on data from the surrounding areas as opposed to the active regions themselves.  The explanation for this discrepancy lies in the presence of longitudinal flows that could be observed in the surrounding areas but not in the active regions.  The researchers found that these longitudinal flows had different patterns depending on whether the active regions were located near the sun's poles or in the middle.  Furthermore, the speed of these waves when moving towards or away from the sun's poles had different patterns depending on whether the active regions were located near the sun's poles or in the middle.

Researchers from the NANOGrav, Parkes, European, and International Pulsar Timing Array Collaborations have discovered strong evidence suggesting a single source for several bracketed frequency bands producing stochastic gravitational wave signals. Approximately $50\%$ to $90\%$ of the total gravitational wave signal in these specific frequency bands is attributed to a particular era lasting from the present to the age of the universe plus a few billion years. The most plausible explanation for this phenomenon is the existence of primordial magnetic fields, followed by a parameter set which points towards an inflationary model known as the $\Lambda$CDM. To further study this hypothesis, researchers have performed an in-depth analysis, simulating data obtained from the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array, to determine how the properties of these primordial magnetic fields can be estimated, while also taking into account a particular limitation of PINTA's current dataset. The simulation yields two key insights: Firstly, despite the presence of significant magnetic fields from the inflationary model, PINTA data does not exhibit a noticeable deviation from the current standard model. Secondly, if the source of the gravitational wave signal is identified as a particular type of burst, PINTA data will be able to pinpoint the exact time of this event along with the minimum possible values for its amplitude and scale.

Light field technology is currently a focal point of interest for the research community due to its capabilities for light field reconstruction and its potential future applications in fields such as computing and display technology. One major challenge posed by these applications is the large amount of data required to represent a light field, with a typical example requiring an enormous 25GB of data. To mitigate this issue, efficient image compression techniques are being developed for practical use. Past solutions, such as the MEF-C and LFI-UC, primarily relied on traditional lossy compression methods like JPEG and other legacy algorithms. In contrast, the proposed model, a disparity-aware model (DAM), utilizes machine learning to derive category-specific patterns and represents a light field as a weighted combination of category-specific sub-baselines, thereby reducing the overall complexity of the light field representation. This method demonstrates superior performance, specifically in terms of rate-distortion metrics, when compared to 14 competing techniques that employ legacy algorithms. Furthermore, the proposed model demonstrates superior qualitative results, with superior quality and reduced complexity. Notably, the proposed model displays an ability to seamlessly integrate with other image compression methods, an observation further emphasized by the results of comparative analysis with the MEF-C method.

In cross-lingual information retrieval using vectors, two fundamental models, 
interactive and non-interactive, have been implemented where query and document 
vectors are normalized through the same method, and different approaches are used 
respectively. This research investigates the advantages of combining these two models 
to improve vector-based cross-lingual information retrieval. Initially, a new 
approach that synchronizes the two models with a common bottleneck layer has been 
introduced to leverage their strengths. Furthermore, a framework has been proposed 
to efficiently evaluate and optimize this combination using a reduced set of data. 
Inspections and observations have been conducted on the initial stages of several 
Bilingual Dictionary Learning models to understand their internal behavior and 
relate them to other known models. Lastly, a comprehensive experiment was 
experimentally verified to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed models in 
boosting the accuracy of vector vector similarity measures when used in 
cross-lingual information retrieval tasks, and supporting findings have been shown 
through additional evidence.

The urgent need for comprehensive health and demographic reports has driven an increased focus on geographic studies, often utilizing detailed, region-based data. Studies essential to track the Sustainable Development Goals frequently rely on combining large-scale surveys, synthetic data, and statistical models with more detailed, localized information from various sources. As a result, researchers face the challenge of merging disparate datasets, thereby necessitating innovative spatial estimation techniques to generate essential indicators at the municipal level. This research brings together three studies that incorporate different approaches to a specific challenge: making informed decisions during an individual data collection process. All studies draw upon a unique setting in Kenya and involve the estimation of various healthcare indicators at the municipal level. They bring different perspectives to this issue, using various statistical methods: (1) utilizing a decision-theoretic framework for a prior selection model for small area estimation in a geographically divided area; (2) incorporating big data for a more accurate estimation of healthcare indicators at the municipal level; and (3) designing an effective sampling strategy for small area estimation. The objective of this study is to propose a semi-classical model representing betting situations where the gambler's winnings are encoded in a quantum memory's intrinsic properties, rather than the conventional payout. We associate the initial investment with a single quantum system's ergotropy - a measure equivalent to the quantum analogue of free energy, as described by Allahverdyan, Balian, and Nieuwenhuizen - and express the randomness of the gamble, typically denoted by $\lambda$, as a measurable shift in the quantum memory's average normalised marginals. This approach is based on a discrete-variable quantum betting framework developed by Pizzirua and Soto, although our analysis relaxes their strict conditions. We relate our semi-classical model to the classic Kelly betting strategy as devised by John L. Kelly. Additionally, our work considers the implications of random $\lambda$ on the gambler's optimal investment amounts, as determined by Janssen - a renowned asymptotic strategy for continuous variable betting. Finally, our study provides an overview of the relationship between the original payoff model and our proposed quantum investment model, as the former corresponds to a specific mean and variance of the $\lambda$ distribution.

Building on the recently created two-dimensional semiconductor MoSi$_2$N$_4$, our comprehensive study of monolayer compounds MA$_2$Z$_4$ involves in-depth analysis of their band structure and excitons using ab initio GW and Bethe-Salpeter equation calculations. In contrast to the predictions of density functional theory, the results of our GW calculations indicate much larger band gaps and quasiparticle energies that are distinct in absolute value but share the same band alignment configurations.

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV and an accumulated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$, yields 4 standard deviation excess beyond predicted background counts with no noticeable features found in dimuon invariant mass spectra.

The magnetic field and non-ideal factors are known to be pivotal in the process of stellar formation, but due to simplicity, hydrodynamics models often take precedence over more accurate representations like the alpha-disk model in major simulations. A recent study proposes a new approach by combining an advanced magnetohydrodynamics model with non-ideal factors and the gravitational potential to explore how the accretion of a massive core results in a nearly stationary protoplanetary disk. With a 2D model that accounts for the disk's rotation, the study reveals that a disk with an average thickness of 8 solar radii forms around the core and that a net angular momentum aligns with expected values. Simulation results show that a disk with a smooth surface and minimal magnetic field can emerge from the core's collapse within 30,000 to 50,000 years. Furthermore, the study finds that a disk with an average distance from the core forms with an exponential rate, and that magnetic effects play a significant role in the disk's edge formation. An investigation of the disk's evolution over 50,000 years in a nearly stationary state revealed that through internal dissipation, the disk's magnetic field will decrease with time, and that a gap will form at the disk's edge due to magnetic effects, however this will not affect the disk's center, thereby allowing for the development of a tilted, asymmetrical shape that can be inherited from the core's rotation. Astronomers rely on atmospheric dispersion corrections to enable telescopic observation in all directions. This correction is typically derived from models of the atmosphere's behavior, which are based on empirical observations. However, these models are only reliable within their established boundaries of validity, and their applicability can change significantly with altitude. In a previous study, we developed an on-solar-spectrum atmospheric dispersion correction method that provides highly accurate results across various atmospheric conditions. This correction method relies on the detection of a telescope's target object, whether it's a star or a planet like the Sun, to calculate precise atmospheric dispersion corrections. This research builds on our previous findings by analyzing how accurately this correction method and others match real atmospheric conditions. By using both a numerical model and actual data collected from the CFHT, we investigated how discrepancies between models and real-world data impact the accuracy of atmospheric dispersion corrections. The results reveal that a previous generation of atmospheric dispersion models, which were established before high-altitude observations, are indeed limited in their applicability to higher elevations. The accuracy of the models was found to decline significantly above 3,500 meters. In response to these findings, we introduced an alternative model that can accurately predict atmospheric dispersion corrections up to elevations of 5,500 meters. This new model provides more precise results, with an average absolute error less than 0.0003 degrees.
