The main contributions of this study include developing an Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme for finding the minimum surface topography (genus and non-orientable genus) for complex network graphs that are densely connected. Densely connected networks are defined by a minimum edge count that exceeds the square of the number of vertices multiplied by a constant greater than 0.5. To achieve this, we first introduce a geometric mapping method that maps diagram surfaces to a sphere for specific surface topologies and then extend this to all possible surface topologies with polynomial-time complexity, approximating the minimum surface topology with an error rate of O(k^-1/π). When the error rate is the other way around, we demonstrate that a mapper can be constructed in polynomial time using the Four-color Theorem. Furthermore, we describe a simple algorithm that finds a surface topology closest to the minimum surface topology with an error rate of O(n^(1/2)) for specific surface topologies and then generalize this to all possible surface topologies with surface genus less than or equal to 1 or non-orientable surface genus less than or equal to 2.

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly minimizing required communication rounds. Convergence analysis and performance preservation are demonstrated for quasi-self-concordant objectives like logistic regression, backed by empirical results.

Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech is outlined, 
having specifically adapted it for use with languages such as Hindi and Bengali 
by leveraging multi-set encoding via word and character representations. 
Given the intricacies of handwritten textual patterns in these languages, 
specific preprocessing techniques were applied to ensure successful training. 
Ultimately, the model exhibited hate-speech identification accuracy of around 
85% on newly presented examples from a range of 1375 samples sourced from 
social media platforms Facebook and Twitter. We found that using transfer 
learning yielded notable gains in accuracy, suggesting potential for the 
identification of more complex textual patterns in these languages.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a dark matter signal originates from space, surpass the neutrino floor, or distinguish between various neutrino sources. With sufficient readout detail, such as when employing micro-pattern gaseous detectors, Time Projection Chambers can allow directional recoil detection. The main issue with these detectors is identifying and eliminating background electron recoils triggered by gamma rays from radioactive substances within the detector and surroundings. We created new indicators that can tell electron and nuclear recoils apart at keV-level energies by using simulated ionization topologies. Our simulations show that these indicators perform significantly better than the traditional dE/Q discriminant, offering up to three times greater differentiation. Additionally, these new indicators remain effective at lower ionization levels below 100 keV and can also be used to identify the direction of recoiling nuclei with high accuracy.

A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior in various contextual situations is essential for accurate risk assessment and mitigation. This study investigates how to effectively combine the strengths of machine learning models and human expertise in commercial driving behavior analysis. Our primary contribution is the development of a collaborative decision-making method, where machine learning predictions are reviewed and validated by human experts to ensure fairness and accuracy in context-specific situations. The proposed strategy involves grounding the algorithm by incorporating real-world scenarios where human input is required to correct or confirm machine learning outputs. The model was trained using a dataset of 385 unique driving scenarios from a fleet management company and was then tested for effectiveness in three separate assessment tasks. The results demonstrate the potential of this collaborative approach to achieve high levels of fairness and accuracy in commercial driving behavior analysis, with the support of human experts. The implemented algorithm achieved an average accuracy of 93% and 86% for objective and fair assessment respectively. It also revealed that the majority of scenarios requiring human review (58.5%) involve contextual factors such as speed and location, which warrant expert examination.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in previously recognized images during testing.
To address this issue, the challenge provided a large dataset obtained from a well-known literary competition and held an accreditation round at an academic conference.
The outcome of the competition revealed several key insights.
First, the top-performing model for verifying recognized text is a basic transformer model.
Furthermore, the research observed that the main difficulty in correctly identifying OOV text lies in the complex word separation, rather than the individual recognition of words.
Ultimately, the outcome of the competition provided valuable guidance to the development of more effective OCR technology in the future.

Random fields in mathematical models depict how interconnected random variables behave over time, influencing a variety of disciplines from statistical physics to system biology. Since their introduction in the 19th century, little has been known about the link between their dynamic behaviors and geometric properties of the underlying spaces they're defined within. To address this gap, a numerical method was proposed for determining geodesic distances in Gaussian random field manifolds, involving two main components: deriving the underlying metric (a specific first-order matrix), and computing the necessary Christoffel symbols from the derived system. These calculations are then used to solve second-order ODEs, providing an accessible analytical solution alongside a numerical method. These approaches were tested using both synthetic and real-world data; the results show that the numerical method is often the more reliable and accurate option. Moreover, applying this framework to multiple practical problems revealed new insights into random field dynamics, allowing for the detection of pattern changes within 90% accuracy and object location precision of five pixels or better.

In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through a vibrating membrane into a heavy fluid layer overlaid by a lighter fluid. This disturbance influences the initial hexagonal structure of the interfacial waves, producing stationary fundamental modes and a set of rolling waves, known as 'herringbones,' which have a specific periodic length. Our research observes and documents the evolution of these interfacial waves over a long period of time. The vibration is specifically adjusted to the natural frequency of the fluid layer, measured to be approximately 1.36 Hz, resulting in a repeating pattern of instability growth every six periods, or three cycles, at the same length as the 'herringbone' waves. We present a comprehensive sequence, captured through images, that illustrates the beginning, middle, and end of this repeating cycle of instability, providing detailed context to our research paper.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ on $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$, the L-function $L(s,F,\chi, E)$ is a Hecke L-function where $E$ is a weight $k$ modular form on which $w$ cyclically shifts the Fourier coefficients of $F$ by raising them to the power of $k$. Given that $k$ is a multiple of the conductor of $\chi$ and at least $2$, the rational numbers $\frac{E(i)}{L(1,F,\chi)}$ and $\frac{2\pi i^{k/2}h(F)}{L(1,F,\chi)}\zeta(1)$ where $h(F)$ is the Hasse-Weil number of $F$ are all similar in proportionality, contained within a bounded set, independent of $F$ and $\chi$. This result is also extended to cusp forms under the same conditions. When combined with a previous study by Diamond and Shin, the outcome yields the common bound of $F$-free zeros of the corresponding Hecke L-functions and a consequence implying that their denominators are also confined to a single, bounded set. Additionally, similar finding hold for the critical values at $i$ of the corresponding L-functions. This result holds true for the L-functions of Hecke and Maass forms coupled with a Dirich

In a tight binding model using the non-equilibrium Green's functions formalism, researchers explored how spin-dependent transport behaves in armchair graphene nanoribbons with ferromagnetic gate control. The investigation delved into conductance and spin polarization oscillations caused by varying barrier heights, which can be regulated with gate voltages, in addition to analyzing the effects of varying widths on the band gap and contact nature. The results show spin polarization oscillates more intensely in nanoribbons with wider band gaps compared to 2D graphene structures, achieving nearly perfect spin polarization in normal-conductor graphene normal-conductor junctions. The distinct transport characteristics of GNRs under the influence of external gates make them suitable for spintronics in device construction.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues in the realm of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to Banach lattices with the power function $|x|^p$ for $1<p\infty$. The key to our approach lies in the Adjoint theorem and a newly described theorem with a relatively simple proof, which to our knowledge has not been previously disclosed. The mentioned theorem bears resemblance to $weakly$-$Lacunary$-$Hyers$-$Robinson$-$Equations properties. The theorem can be summed up by the following statement: For aadditively perfomed functions $f,g$, and multiplicative function $h$ on a Banach lattice, their corresponding mappings $F, G, H$ satisfy the condition $F(x)+G(y)+H(\frac{xy}{x+y})=\frac{f(x)+g(y)}{x+y}$. This property gives rise to specific operator theorems. Theorems analogous to Korovkin can be derived from the weakly nonlinear, monotone operators acting on the Banach lattice with the power function $|x|^p$ for $1<p\infty$. A graph on n vertices is called pancyclic if it contains a cycle of every possible length from 3 to n. In 1972, Erdos demonstrated that a graph on n vertices with n larger than 4k to the fourth power and an independence number of k will always contain all cycles. After his findings, he suggested the independence number squared value should also be sufficient for this, later proven otherwise by subsequent results and further improved upon by the presented work which now shows that there exists a constant c, that n being larger than ck to the 7/3 power guarantees a pancyclic structure.

The trajectory of light particles created in gold-gold, ruthenium-ruthenium, and zirconium-zirconium collisions at a specific energy level of 200 GeV has been studied in this research. This study utilized the CLVisc model to examine the development of uneven energy density, pressure variations, and radial movement along a specific axis, finding significant relationships among these elements. By comparing data on specific particles to laboratory collisions, researchers discovered that an initial moment of the energy density is linked to the movement of light particles, both positive and negative. This moment also correlates with the movement of protons and antiprotons, but to a lesser extent. In contrast, pressure variations were found to be associated solely with the movement of positive particles. A statistical analysis showed that the movement of particles that are symmetric has a stronger connection to the movement of particles overall. This study found that initial conditions of pressure and energy density are both linked to the movement of particles, but to different degrees.

The adaptive spectral Koopman method (AKM) is an evolution equation-based technique for modeling complex systems, offering high precision with minimal data requirements. It has been effective in scenarios involving nonlinearity and irregular system components. However, these systems often involve parts with different characteristics, such as stable or unstable areas. Further, irregular systems may appear smooth due to a high dimensional structure, misleading the assumption of a low-dimensional embedding. Addressing these issues, we integrate the AKM with sparse-grid techniques to create a new method capable of handling high dimensional structures and dimensional bottlenecks in complex systems. This combination, called the sparse-grid-based adaptive spectral Koopman method (SKAKM), is tested on numerical examples, demonstrating improved performance in low-dimensional embedding and accurately predicting long-term system behavior. Additionally, SKAKM is compared to the standard AKM, highlighting that the former often yields more precise results with less computational cost. Finally, we discuss the current limitations of SKAKM and propose potential areas for further exploration.

This review provides an overview of quantum mechanics history with a specific focus on addressing the theoretical difficulties in explaining ionization within the framework of quantum mechanics. The fundamental principles of resonance theory are then explored, and how they have informed the development of exterior complex scaling to efficiently describe the continuum in large systems like molecules. Exterior complex scaling is a highly effective technique with a proven ability to accurately predict strong-field ionization, and we will also see how it has been further modified into an improved method called regional complex scaling. We will see that this variant has its own set of advantages, and has been outperformed by a different variant called local complex scaling in certain instances. The practicalities of implementing exterior complex scaling in computer code will also be explored, and we will see how a theoretical model for non-perturbative resonance widths has evolved over time with key advances in the field. The final section of this review will be dedicated to outlining the remaining challenges in this area of research.

The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a widely-used solution to the Schrödinger problem. While it's well-documented that this algorithm converges when a solution exists, a linear convergence rate is achieved only if both the solution and the function in question are strictly positive. If either of these conditions is not met, the algorithm simply calculates an approximation. This paper reveals that even without a solution, the Sinkhorn algorithm still converges toward the best possible approximation under specified marginal constraints. Furthermore, we provide a method for determining when these constraints can be satisfied and demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm in a numerical example.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recorded data of 257 pb-1 in proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV centre-of-mass energy in 2017, which was used to determine the t¯t cross-section. The measurement, based on an event sample featuring one isolated electron and one isolated muon, has a uncertainty of 3.9% and was found to be $\sigma$t¯t = 43.4 ± 3.0 pb, in line with theoretical predictions. The data also confirms the consistency of t¯t production with next-to-leading-order quantum chromodynamics.

It's logical to assume that the characteristics of a surrounding system or environment would influence the properties of its central partner, but the extent of this impact remains complex and not fully understood. Researchers have recently created a novel model that includes a central harmonic oscillator linked to a one-dimensional bath through a spring with adjustable stiffness. Conducting numerical experiments for a wide range of parameters, including our own previous studies, allows us to compare the results to theoretical predictions derived from the average influence approximation. Interestingly, when the surrounding system conveys energy to the central oscillator, the central oscillator's fluctuations are similar to those of an independent central oscillator. However, when the central oscillator's energy is transferred to the surrounding system, the surrounding system's fluctuations are substantially greater than those of an independent system, yet the central oscillator's fluctuations are lower than expected. These unexpected findings are related to key characteristics of the surrounding system. For instance, when the central oscillator's energy is transferred to the surrounding system, the surrounding system's fluctuations are significantly greater than those of an independent system. Conversely, when the surrounding system conveys energy to the central oscillator, the surrounding system's fluctuations are substantially lower than those of an independent system. Additionally, our research indicates that when the central oscillator's energy is transferred to the surrounding system, the surrounding system's fluctuations are higher than expected when the central oscillator is in its localized state. However, when the central oscillator is in its delocalized state, the surrounding system's fluctuations are less than expected.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting the question of whether these changes persisted after mobility restrictions were lifted. To address this question, our research analyzed how individuals' daily routines changed during the pandemic and its aftermath, using data from mobile devices, and quantified the diversity of urban encounters in Chicago. We found that the pandemic led to an increase in meeting places from an average of 0.196 to 0.232 (standard deviation of 0.001 and 0.006, respectively) and a decrease in encounter diversity. While encounters became more diverse in terms of location, they became less diverse in terms of social context. This decline in diversity persisted even six months after mobility restrictions were lifted, likely due to increased fear of infection and subsequent changes in personal behavior. Our research provides early evidence of how the pandemic transformed urban social patterns, highlighting the need for ongoing monitoring of these changes to better understand the long-term impact of pandemics on urban planning and planning scientists' decision-making abilities.

This research project focuses on the advancement of a nonlinear field-split
preconditioner comprising two stages to expedite convergence of complex two-phase
fluid dynamics and transport within diverse porous media. A proposed algorithm,
Field-Split Multiplicative Schwarz Newton, operates in a sequential two-step process:
initially, an approximate update of pressure and saturation is achieved through
a preconditioning step by resolving sub-problems in succession; secondly, a
global Newton update is applied at the preconditioned values via system linearization.
Using demanding case studies, the FSMSN approach was compared against established
methods including MSPIN and conventional strategies like Sequential Fully Implicit
and Fully Implicit Methods. Notably, the analysis included examination of the
sensitivity of computational performance to the discrete size of the problem and
local disorder of the porous media in the test scenarios. Results indicated that
the FSMSN preconditioning technique exhibited computational domain instability
tendencies, though yielding notable reductions in computational time across a wide
range of challenging problem sets. Field-split preconditioning methods showed
capacity to bypass intricate linear systems solutions typically linked with implicit
preconditioning while maintaining local stability, albeit subject to potential
domain-wide instability hazards. Further optimizations were identified as being
necessary for accurate computation in highly disordered media environments.

discrete matrix realm, though a clear strategy for managing computational time

The property of chirality exists ubiquitously in various sizes of geometric patterns - ranging from organic life to molecular structures - across different scales. Chiral matter responds to chiral light with specific polarization properties that allow for the identification and separation of enantiomers, which are key components in pharmaceutical preparations. Chiral optical cavities can amplify specific chiral light wavelengths while rejecting others with opposing polarization properties, but all previous implementations using handheld tools have not exhibited inherent chirality due to the use of linear hands. This limitation has been overcome by proposing and testing a new type of optical cavity called the single-handedness chiral cavity. Our research involves constructing this innovative SOC cavity using locally resonant metamaterials and confirming its ability to amplify specific chiral light wavelengths while rejecting others with opposing polarization properties, which paves the way for applications such as polarization-sensitive plasmonics, chiral photonics, and handheld devices for identifying and separating enantiomers.

This paper examines the connection between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity on anti de-Sitter spaces and a semi-classical limit of two-dimensional string theory, with c less than 1. We observe that the world-sheet theory of this string theory, comprising a space-like Liouville CFT and a time-like non-compact fermion F, shares similarities with the previous findings. Like the results of He'neaux and Rajabakhsh, we identify the partition function of this three-dimensional JT gravity as the product of two distinct sums. One sum involves the spectrum associated with the duality couple (F, Liouville), while the other replicates the spectral representation of the gravitational modes. We also replicate the behavior of the gravitational wave functions in terms of the duality couple (F, Liouville). Furthermore, we replicate the observed relationship between the gravitational wave functions and the random geometry characterized by the boundary of the three-dimensional JT gravity with a negative cosmological constant and two singular points. This replication involves the replication of the replica symmetry of the random Hamiltonian associated with the duality couple (F, Liouville), which governs the energy spectrum of the random eigenvalues located at the two singular points.

A spacetime distortion, or warp bubble, generated by the Alcubierre metric can enable massive objects to achieve global speeds faster than light. This research extends our previous solutions by applying the Einstein equations to the warp drive metric, incorporating both a perfect fluid source and a perfect fluid source with a cosmological constant, including a special case with a perfect fluid source and no cosmological constant, previously found by the researchers ( arXiv:2101.11467 ). These new solutions have led to the connection between warp drive, shock waves, and Burgers equations, via a perfect fluid source without a cosmological constant ( arXiv:2008.06560 ), as well as analysis of the various energy conditions in the Einstein equations. However, it seems the shift vector, required to achieve warp speeds, requires an intricate arrangement of matter, energy and momentum within the spacetime. This implies achieving warp speeds using Alcubierre spacetime geometry would necessitate a highly complex and sophisticated arrangement of matter in order to produce warp drive, although this may be achievable through stable matter distribution that meets the requirements of the Einstein equations.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing upkeep, cities are faced with the challenge of coordinating maintenance, predicting and resolving issues, and fulfilling their goal of becoming smart cities due to limited understanding of their infrastructure's current state. Most cities lack accurate digital data on their underground systems (electricity, water, natural gas), hindering construction project planning. To overcome these issues, a common framework is needed to manage and process the various types of data cities collect and need to analyze. To address this, the GUIDES platform was developed to combine different city data management components. This proposal showcases GUIDES' capabilities with Birmingham, UK as the case study, highlighting its top features: mapping underground infrastructure; creating 3D geospatial models; and developing web platforms and mobile apps for data visualization and citizen reporting. GUIDES allows cities to easily access, on-demand, the data management tools and tools for data analysis, modification, and distribution as needed. Birmingham's integration of these systems demonstrated significant ROI in its city data management.

To analyze the center-of-mass motion of hundreds of $^9$Be$^+$ ions, arranged in a two-dimensional Wigner crystal, we utilized the interaction between optical dipoles and the ions' spin, enabling the mapping of their kinematic states. By examining the effects of a specific trapping parameter on the observed motion, we determined that the prevailing mode-temperature relationship in these crystals remains unchanged from previous findings in smaller systems. Furthermore, we conducted a comprehensive examination of the ion ensemble's state of motion by analyzing the spin ensemble's dephasing behavior. Our investigation discovered that the ion crystal's temperature, which is primarily due to the collective motion of the particles, can be accurately inferred from the rate of loss spawned by this motion. Conversely, when the collective motion is damped, the temperature assessment becomes inaccurate and instead measures the individual vibrations of the particles. Additionally, the frequency spectrum of the ion crystal's motion contains valuable information about its thermal state.

TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces with subnanometer resolution. Yet, accurately simulating specific TERS signals is computationally difficult. Our innovative method combines the primary factors driving the effectiveness of TERS, the electromagnetic and chemical interactions, into a single simulation. The electromagnetic influence describes the sample's interaction with highly localized, inhomogeneous electric fields produced by the plasmonic tip, a focal point of many mechanistic studies. Conversely, the chemical interaction accounts for the distinct responses between the apex tip and sample under extremely close-range, highly position-sensitive chemical interactions. Our study focuses on a quantum mechanical model where the apex tip, sample, and tip's electromagnetic fields are fully resolved. The results show the sample's wave function, electromagnetic fields, and resulting Raman signals highly depend on the specific chemical and electromagnetic connections between the apex tip and sample orbitals. These findings significantly enhance our comprehension of the physical drivers behind Raman signals at the atomic or molecular level and enable more precise simulation of Raman signals. The algorithm developed here can be used for a wide range of simulations in near-field spectroscopy.

We used the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope to study the emission of nearby spiral galaxies in the K-band through a 6 GHz bandwidth observation. Our goal was to detect the Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) produced by spinning dust grains in the galaxies NGC 3627, NGC 4254, NGC 4736, and NGC 5055, with particular focus on the AME signal correlated with thermal dust emission. We carried out two observations at 23.8 GHz, achieving an average noise level of approximately 12.6 Jy and 20.4 Jy respectively, allowing us to place an upper limit on the AME flux density relative to the thermal dust flux. We considered a range of spectral indices for the AME and thermal dust components, finding no evidence for AME when compared with previous data sets. Our upper limits on the AME-to-thermal dust flux ratio, expressed as a function of frequency, are consistent with models of interstellar dust.

Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies a significant ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by an exceptionally large entropy variation and both electrocaloric and barocaloric properties. For decades, researchers have disputed the underlying cause of the significant entropy change, but this issue is now resolved using a comprehensive approach that incorporates density functional theory-based phonon calculations, inelastic neutron scattering, and additional neutron scattering experiments. In contrast to the previously assumed, albeit widely adopted model of entropy involving disorder across the high-symmetry phase's mirror plane, it is now clear that this simplistic model is invalid. Instead, it is discovered that the significant entropy originates from the low-frequency wobbling of ammonium ions in this phase, which produces small to negligible harmonic components along the corresponding axis. These findings also support the presence of corresponding soft modes at temperatures below the phase transition. Furthermore, it is found that the displacement of the ammonium ions in the low-symmetry phase is more complex than previously considered, involving rotation and vibration. These results hold significant implications for the analysis of various solid-state phenomena involving frequency-dependent disorder and offer insights into the use of molecular systems as functional materials.

In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a less than optimal strategy known as probability-matching, which means choosing options based on their reward probabilities, as opposed to the optimal strategy, maximization, which involves consistently selecting the option with the highest reward.  Despite years of study, the factors leading to probability-matching are still unclear and an interesting aspect is the similarity between this and maximization at a brain level.  We provide evidence that explains a range of behaviors by developing different models and show that a specific model which is sub-optimal and recurring appears to be related to the way the brain processes errors in prediction.  We found that there are specific brain regions that distinguish between these two prediction error signals and this difference corresponds with the factors that influence the probability-matching phenomenon.  In our study, participants performed a learning task with visual and auditory components and we analyzed their brain activity while they played either a game that gives the same reward for winning or losing (fixed-win/loss ratio) or a game that gives different rewards for winning and losing (variable-win/loss ratio).  We found that the probability of making the best choice with the highest reward (optimism index) and the accuracy of estimating the value of winning or losing (center of mass model index) correlated with specific brain activity in the mesencephalon, a brain structure known to be involved in reward processing. A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems based on a dodecahedron's geometry, to study quantum mechanics' nonlocality and contextuality. An alternative setup using 120 states is examined in this work. Despite their different sizes, both arrangements are linked to a common 8D lattice with 240 fundamental vectors, tied to the E8 Lie algebra. An exploration of this setup's properties employs many comparisons to the Witting configuration's attributes.

The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem involves precomputing a data structure that efficiently finds closest polygonal curves within a certain radius from query curves, considering an approximation factor for potential inaccuracies. This study primarily investigates this problem using time series curves, providing a comprehensive analysis for one-dimensional curves. By improving existing results, the research offers multiple contributions: multiple tradeoffs between approximation quality, preprocessing efficiency, and query speed; a near-optimal analysis of an earlier proposal; and the first examination of the tradeoffs for allowing query curves to be unapproximated for precision. The research sets new limits for achieving approximate near neighbor search while reducing the impact of approximation factors and demonstrates that approximate near neighbor search can be as efficient as its exact counterpart, up to certain limits, for specific curve types and distance metrics.

To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between efficiency and effectiveness: methods offering higher efficiency tend to be less effective and vice versa. In response, this research aims to eliminate this efficiency versus effectiveness tradeoff by introducing a new MEM strategy that combines unconventional noise modeling and a detailed analysis of the outcome distribution through unfolding. We demonstrate this approach on a specific circuit used to generate superposition states and compare it to existing methods. Moreover, this research is compatible with current state-of-the-art implementation methods and can be easily scaled up to accommodate a much wider range of systems.

When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently necessary for the robot to infer which task to perform. In situations where task instructions are ambiguous, a major difficulty arises for the robot arm, as it must decide between several possible actions. The problem is compounded when the desired action necessitates significant movement along a force field, as this makes it more challenging for the human to grasp the intended tool within the workspace. A novel system for shared control has been developed to alleviate these issues. The system allows humans to convey specific "conventions" to the robot, where conventions are defined as specific task-related parameters (such as a point, a vector, or a shape) associated with a particular action. Through an analysis of the robot's operating history, an inference model has been developed to anticipate which action the human intends to perform, given the submitted convention. The model trains an decision tree that predicts the likely convention submitted by the human for a given action, where this prediction is based on both the submitted convention and the submitted action. Three distinct methods for learning the decision tree have been explored: supervision, self-learning, and adversarial learning. The system has been evaluated through an experiment conducted in a virtual environment, where participants either used conventional tools or unconventional devices to complete tasks. Where conventional tools were used, the system could reach an average accuracy of 83.44% for predicting the likely submitted convention. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is proposed, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance and avoids attempting to build a global map in unfamiliar environments. As a result, this system is capable of reducing mapping errors caused by movement inaccuracies. In addition to preventing global mapping issues, HiTMap also integrates a new localization system called HiTLoc, which performs localization based on the local map instead of a global map. In comparison to existing state-of-the-art localization and mapping techniques, HiTMap and HiTLoc demonstrate comparable or even superior performance while requiring significantly fewer computational resources and showcasing stable and consistent results throughout our experiments.

Research into two-dimensional arrays with favorable two-dimensional correlation properties has gained significant interest due to the rapid advancements in modern wireless communication technologies. Various applications of two-dimensional arrays can be found in areas such as ultra-wide band, 2-D synchronization, and phased array antennas. This paper presents a novel method for creating two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets by utilizing multivariable functions to overcome the limitations of inter-group complementary code sets. As a result, two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets can be constructed with fewer data points, and with either a two-dimensional or one-dimensional synchronization structure, thereby expanding the possibilities for their applications in wireless communication technologies.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. In addition to these physical principles, CT data is often corrupted by electronic noise generated from detectors. A critical application of CT scans involves differentiating materials within which images are taken, such as in bone and calcium analysis. However, the denoising process commonly employed can cause image detail loss, which poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, this study presents a new variational reconstruction model that effectively combines multiple energy-level CT data denoising and clear differentiation of materials with a built-in prior that favors image consistency and clarity. Our proposed model, detailed in Section 2, incorporates a new regularization term, its mathematical formulation and the role of its components are explained. Our findings from various numerical experiments are presented in Section 3, which demonstrate the effectiveness and practicality of our proposed model.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local approach that excludes the spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi approximation by considering an equivalent reduced gap size.

In this research, we investigate the user's part in Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER), revealing (1) that humans outperform automated methods in finding suitable entities, and (2) that instructing users to focus on sentence segments containing the target entity's name yields better retrieval and fewer assessments needed. This insight drives our proposal of a new method for CNER, which initially presents users with a full text context, then asks for a sub-set of relevant segments, and finally retrieves entities based on those selections. Our proposed approach outperforms existing CNER tools in various evaluation scenarios and adapts well to scenarios with limited user interaction. This research is conducted within the framework of a large-scale user study focusing on identifying and retrieving entities related to significant public events, such as the Covid-19 pandemic and the European Championship football tournament.

Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, giving it a distinct structural context that forms the foundation of its constituent parts. When dealing with multi-variable data sets that change over time, we anticipate observing interconnected patterns, long-term fluctuations, seasonal variations, and correlations across different variables. In contrast, longitudinal data often displays relationships between and within individual units over time, including both intra- and inter-subject correlations. While analyzing time series and longitudinal data differs in certain aspects, they frequently employ similar visual display methods. Our approach focuses on creating an interactive framework that allows users to explore and dissect the time-based components of these data types, including how to transform and manipulate the data. Many time-based visualizations can be directly applied, with additional features necessary for distinct data types. Our methodology incorporates the flexible use of time limits, data filtering, and highlightable elements to facilitate detailed examination. We provide an interactive environment with dynamic views, including small multiple displays, long-term fluctuations, and a chronological overview, enabling users to accurately understand both the entire data set and its individual components.

The promising potential of extracting valuable insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has emerged as a crucial area of study, as machine learning models can assist healthcare professionals in decision-making to enhance overall healthcare quality. Advances in recent years have seen the integration of deep learning models into clinical settings, although most current approaches focus exclusively on sequential data within EHRs. We propose a novel graph neural network framework called HeteroSim-GNN that efficiently utilizes diverse similarity information between healthcare entities. By incorporating domain experts' knowledge to calculate similarities between different healthcare entities, we have successfully improved the accuracy of diagnosis classification from raw EHR data. From a practical standpoint, we have constructed a large-scale real-world dataset from EHR records, as well as developed a collaborative platform for multiple healthcare institutions to analyze and compare similar clinical cases. The framework and code will be made publicly available to the research community through a GitHub repository, while the dataset will be hosted on the Open Data eHealth platform for other researchers to access.

Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle size and charge, we model a electric double layer (EDL) formed around a soft, charge-bearing material in an solvent containing identical, mobile ions. By writing the interaction between the material and ions based on a modified version of the Carnahan and Starling equation, we derive equations for the EDL charge distribution, density of ions near the material, and diffusion potential. Our analysis shows that the way ions pack themselves near the material is affected by the material's size and non-uniform charge distribution. This packing influences the material's potential energy and electric field, causing self-attractive forces and positively charged surfaces to experience a repulsive effect. Additionally, we find that the material's surface charge density is affected by its size and non-uniform charge distribution, and this influence also impacts the diffusion potential. Finally, our analysis reveals that the material's electric field decreases as it nears its point of highest charge density. This decrease is particularly pronounced at the highest levels of non-uniform charge.

Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for many researchers. To this end, we have developed a comprehensive pipeline that leverages cutting-edge natural language processing techniques, including tokenization, part-of-speech analysis, and deep learning algorithms, to accurately extract and identify requirements from text. Our work builds on the advances made in this field by training and integrating multiple models to enhance the precision of requirement extraction. Moreover, we have adapted a state-of-the-art transformer model to play a proactive role in identifying requirements through both sequential and attention-based mechanisms. Given the recent transformer-based breakthroughs in machine translation tasks, we argue that the transformer model offers significant advantages for requirement extraction tasks. Ultimately, we propose a novel dataset derived from open-source Java projects, dubbed JRRE, to support further advancements in this field through comparative studies and to foster the development of more efficient data science tools. To facilitate future advancements, we provide a JRRE dataset version 2 with updated requirements, tokenized texts, and deep learning model training data, available on GitHub at https://github.com/tony431963/jrre.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a maximum diversity network coding technique. A direct link between outage probability, energy consumption, and energy efficiency is established, followed by a formulation of the optimization problem to maximize energy efficiency under the constraint of maintaining a target outage probability. A practical scheduling and power allocation strategy is implemented to minimize power usage. Since the optimization problem is complex and difficult to solve, a tight approximation is first used to simplify the outage probability, then energy efficiency is re-expressed in a different form and the optimization problem is re-cast into a solvable form as a mixed-integer non-linear problem. A generalized outer approximation algorithm is then applied to find a solution that simultaneously optimizes scheduling and power allocation, showing how to obtain the best possible energy efficiency gains by optimizing these two strategies. A comparison with a no network coding scheme shows that with a smaller number of relays, it's beneficial to use no network coding to minimize power usage; but when the relay density increases, it's more beneficial to use all the relays to transmit simultaneously to maximize diversity and thus reduce power usage.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local density of states for precise analysis. Utilizing detailed simulations, the model predicts that YSR states exhibit distinct splittings proportional to their orbital angular momentum and influenced by spin-orbit interactions. Furthermore, the model suggests that YSR states in a spin-orbit material may exhibit YSR state splitting proportional to their orbital angular momentum and independent of their spin polarity under conditions of equal electron and hole superconducting gaps. Additionally, the model simulates the case of two Mn impurities separated by a single Nb atom on the Nb(110) surface, observing a distinct splitting of the YSR states that are not spin-polarized and showing agreement with experimental results.

Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) can efficiently register and accurately bound point cloud errors for scenes without moving objects.  However, traditional methods in the field struggle when it comes to scenes with significant changes in view.  To improve performance in these cases, deep learning-based approaches have shown potential, but often come with limited explanations for their results.  This research introduces a new method that addresses the issue of reducing bias in deep learning-based point cloud registration, providing key insights into its design.  The proposed approach involves a residual network that accounts for positional bias during registration and has been shown to be effective when applied in combination with other deep learning-based methods.  Notably, the new residual network performed well when used alone, with an average Hausdorff distance of less than 0.02 meters when registering 40,350 scans from the ICL dataset.

Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, encompassing 
agriculture, navigation, and urban planning, often resulting in immense 
databases requiring extensive computational power for processing. Deep 
learning methods have recently gained traction for analyzing satellite images. 
Although these methods deliver optimal results, they incur significant CPU 
and GPU utilization. This paper presents an alternative approach utilizing 
the Enhancement-Edge-Extract (EEE) framework, combining three components: 
Enhancement, Edge, and Extract. The Enhancement module upgrades image quality, 
the Edge module identifies and trims out noisy edges, and the Extract module 
isolates and amplifies desired visual elements. The EEE framework is then 
combined with a feature generator for semantic edge detection. The proposed 
approach offers a balance between performance and speed, remaining competitive 
when compared to deep learning methods and surpassing them in energy efficiency.

Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes significant electronic excitation, triggering rapid changes within the material's electronic system that occur over the time frame of a few femtoseconds. This dynamic process, governed by electronic relaxation and interaction with the intense X-ray pulse, has been largely studied using semi-classical models that describe changes in the material's absorption cross-section when probed by X-rays. An alternative to these semi-classical models is offered by quantum models, but such approaches have yet to be applied due to their inherent complexity. This work presents a simplified rate equation model that describes the progression of the material's electronic state from a initial ground state to a final fully-ionized state. This rate equation model serves as an interface with quantum models of valence shell excitation, establishing a connection that allows for the incorporation of multi-scattering events, along with other effects, in schemes that involve multiple elemental components. This multi-phonon rate equation model has been successfully applied to a range of soft and hard materials that are either in a liquid or solid state and also analyzed under both static and dynamic conditions. The results obtained match those of quantum models, demonstrating the model's utility for the analysis of soft and hard materials that are either in a liquid or solid state, particularly for the analysis of multi-phonon rate equations that may be relevant in the context of electron-phonon coupling in the relaxation and absorption dynamics of

The application of a Deep Neural Network in Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional methods even in harsh wireless environments, but this can be compromised by targeted adversarial attacks that inject noise into wireless channels. This paper presents a new method based on a generative adversarial network (GAN) designed to mitigate the effects of such attacks by removing malicious interference before feeding data into a DNN-based classifier. The proposed approach specifically protects AMC systems from attacks like the Fast-Gradient Sign method. The existing GAN countermeasures were ineffective when adapted for AMC tasks due to diverse modulation orders and suboptimal data preparation. This research therefore developed a new method by combining a DNN-based data mixer to minimize malicious distortions with a class discriminator that ensures data integrity. The proposed approach was tested through simulation on various wireless channels and compared to a baseline DNN without GAN countermeasures, showing improved accuracy by 25% against the Fast-Gradient Sign attack.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that experts struggle with.
Recent studies propose using artificial intelligence-based techniques but most
models are one-dimensional as they rely on a single, large dataset, which is
not adaptable. A more effective approach would be for the model to continuously
learn and improve its ability to identify lesion characteristics as it's exposed
to datasets from different hospitals sequentially. We examine the potential of
experience replay, a notable method in the field of artificial intelligence,
specifically within the context of segmenting lesions using imaging data from 8
different hospitals. Our experiments confirm that experience replay achieves a
beneficial effect by maintaining the segmentation accuracy of a model that's
been trained on a sequence of several datasets from different hospitals.
Comparing the results to a model that's been trained in a traditional,
batch-style approach shows that experience replay achieves a valuable advantage of
6-13% when assessing overall lesion segmentation precision and visual quality
metrics. Furthermore, using experience replay reduces the need for large,
batch-trained datasets, allowing for more manageable training sets of just 10%
less inaccurate than batch-trained models. Ultimately, our results indicate
that experience replay is an efficient technique for segmenting lesions that can
be applied in real-world scenarios.

A novel type of metric comparison analogous to Alexandrov comparison is established, 
and its relationship to optimal transport between measures on a Riemannian manifold 
is demonstrated, specifically with respect to the MTW condition proposed by Xi-Nan 
Ma, Neil Trudinger and Xu-Jia Wang, involving a notion of continuity.

Across various disciplines, there's considerable interest in creating predictive models for complex systems using data. To tackle this, we've developed an integrated framework that combines data-driven learning and domain knowledge to identify complex systems even with limited, noisy observations. This framework can be applied to different machine learning models, both continuous and discrete, and handles different types of model errors. After establishing a foundation in the field of model error reduction, we explore the utility of a machine learning approach for identifying and learning errors in model reductions. Specifically, we've developed methods to estimate parameters in the Taylor series basis using least squares and support vector regression. We've tested our methods with a simplified model of climate systems and seen positive results, suggesting that this approach could effectively leverage machine learning to improve model reduction results.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows - specifically, those that have a higher mass concentration, defined by the mass-to-radius ratio. Compared to others, these cores are more massive and have a higher density, suggesting they play a crucial role in the formation of massive stars. This finding supports the theory that massive stars originate from more substantial molecular cores. Furthermore, a core's velocity dispersion exhibits a consistent relationship with its radius, consistent with predictions from magnetohydrodynamic models, implying that magnetism dominates the core's dynamics. Lastly, a comparison of the cores' positions with those of protostellar candidates indicates that massive stars are more likely to emerge from more concentrated cores.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible explanation for dark matter, particularly in models where the universal gravitational potential is influenced by a long-range $(1/r)$ potential. If these black holes exist, they would primarily be found in areas with low density and high pressure, such as in regions where the gravitational potential allows for further segregation. To study the statistical properties of these black holes, we utilize simulations that model the separation of primordial black holes based on their masses and spatial distribution, and these properties are reflected in the mass function, which correlates with local density and fluctuations in the universe. Our PopSyCLE model offers a parameterized approach to studying these black holes based on the masses of their primordial scalar inflaton roots, which can be varied to model different scenarios, such as a single peak of primordial black holes, a bimodal distribution, or multiple peaks. In addition to considering monopole moments, we also model the separation of primordial black holes with quadrupole moments, which has a significant impact on the mass function, particularly on smaller scales, leading to a local underabundance and a global overabundance of primordial black holes, and this effect is more pronounced for larger black holes, with smaller haloes underabundant and massive haloes overabundant, with these trends continuing with larger cosmic structures. We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of uniform wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo simulations, where each molecule consisted of six aligned spheres of gradually decreasing sizes, and the shape of these molecules was defined solely by the ratio of the smallest to the largest sphere diameters, referred to as parameter $d$. The systems' phases were studied as a function of parameter $d$ and the packing density of molecules $\eta$, under the condition that only repulsive interactions were present. This led to the system's behavior being controlled solely by the entropy of molecular arrangement. For systems where the packing density was below $0.5$, in addition to the standard liquid state, we observed standard nematic and smectic A liquid crystalline phases. Conversely, when the packing density exceeded $0.5$, two distinct non-standard liquid states and a polar smectic A phase emerged. The non-standard liquid states were characterized by layers that alternated between pure nematic and molecular tilt directions within each layer, referred to as the polar polar and splay modulated liquids. In order to distinguish between these two liquid states, we studied the melting of smectic A phases as a function of parameter $d$ and packing density. This research revealed that the melting of modulated liquid is related to specific rules that govern the ordering process, as opposed to the conventional ordering process of conventional liquid crystals. Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator and classification tokens in BERT, just before self-attention operations in each Transformer layer.
By doing this, PASTA updates a tiny fraction of the model's parameters and we can implement it without complicated hyperparameter optimization. We evaluated PASTA on benchmark datasets like GLUE and imSOS for NLP tasks and MindSponge for computer vision tasks, comparing its performance with other parameter-efficient tuning methods.
The results show that PASTA achieves comparable performance to the baseline model when the pre-trained model was fine-tuned on the target dataset, and even outperforms model averaging in some cases.
What's more, our proposal has several advantages. For example, PASTA requires no additional hyperparameters and does not need to update the model's weights and attention mechanisms, just the special token embeddings.
This approach also simplifies data parallel training and distributed tuning. Moreover, our proposal of updating the special token embeddings for each label in multi-class datasets could potentially outperform model averaging.

This paper investigates a complex problem where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection. The inherent nature of this problem prevents us from making absolute preferences between options, which prompts the use of context-dependent preference modeling. To tackle this issue, we examine two distinct Siamese network designs, contrasting one that compares the resultant collections after an addition with another that considers each item's individual contribution to the existing collection. Through experiments involving a real-world task of learning Magic: The Gathering deck-building card preferences, we found that the triplet network outperformed its counterpart and surpassed previous performance levels in this area.

Our application of the lattice cluster theory for a significant number of polymer models has led to new insights about the connection between thermodynamic properties and the process of glass formation. This has enabled us to assess the impact of temperature on the latent nature of the glass transition and to investigate the dynamic properties through the application of mode-coupling theory. The primary discovery is a common pattern among our tested models, which involves decreasing intensity in the mode-coupling theory correlations as the residual vibrational entropy approaches zero from higher values. Additionally, we found that there is an correlation between this phenomenon and the displacement of the dynamic property distributions from their most extreme positions as the temperature at which slow dynamics occurs decreases. Meanwhile, the latent nature of the transition remains unaffected by temperature but directly related to the strength of the interactions between molecules.

Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, especially when it involves negation. Unlike previous studies, our research delves into how these models process negation during language acquisition. We've identified a pattern in how they handle negation consistently throughout different tasks, which often leads to incorrect solutions for logical problems. When rewriting problem statements to exclude the negation, or by incorporating examples of both affirming and denying sentences into a context window, the model's performance improves, indicating that its ability to handle negation is superficial or limited to specific surface-level patterns. This reveals a significant flaw in the capability of state-of-the-art language models to reason and understand language.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on globalization. We'll demonstrate how curvature graph weights can be explicitly defined through a hypergeometric function and an even simpler expression that combines it with a formula for the underlying connection graph weights. Notably, we examine a cotangent bundle case, leading to a substantial simplification of the curvature expression.

This research involves determining the large N limit of $O(N)$ models at all values of the coupling strength, which includes an interesting interaction of imaginary units. We use this derivation to investigate how thermal entropy in the JJ model relates to entanglement entropy, finding that it matches the behavior expected in such systems. In contrast, the traditional AdS/CFT approach falls short for all coupling strengths, whereas our results confirm that there's a common underlying dynamic with a quark-gluon plasma in the JJ regime that also exists in systems with non-negative imaginary mass. This reveals that certain characteristics of a non-relativistic system can also be seen in its relativistic counterpart.

Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution in 2015 with the development of a universal framework for pricing Asian options based on one-dimensional Markov processes. This note applies the framework to a modified variant of the model in art: artists as markets (AR) developed by Argeris, Evrigenma, and Zanette. Additionally, we provide a detailed comparison between the two models, highlighting similarities and differences. Notably, we observe that despite similarities in pricing theory, the practical implementation and advantages vary significantly between the two models.

The source behind the diffuse gamma-ray background is currently unknown. However, various galactic features such as star-forming and starburst galaxy clusters may hold the answer. A proposed study suggests that galaxy clusters could be the origin of the diffuse gamma-ray background due to the accumulation of secondary cosmic rays and dark matter annihilation products. This possibility is explored through a hypothetical scenario where both the infrared and gamma-ray spectra of clusters match observed patterns. This scenario is consistent with a given energy distribution and constraints on cosmic rays and neutrino properties, indicating a 12% to 34% likelihood. This likelihood translates to a 9% to 41% probability that galaxy clusters produce the diffuse gamma-ray background alone. Additionally, this theory results in a predicted rate of particle astrophysics experiments' kiloparsec-scale nearest galaxy pair neutrino observations. This rate needs to be verified through future experiments.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we look at any sharp feature within an inflationary model. These features can induce unsuppressed quantum fluctuations in heavy fields, leaving detectable signatures in primordial non-Gaussian patterns, and revealing details about the spectra of these heavy degrees of freedom.

Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be particularly challenging. To address this issue, a framework called LaViSE is proposed to enable convolutional neural networks to describe their internal workings in plain text. By using generic image data, this approach develops a way to map complex image features to simple words, which can then be used to explain any visual model. The performance of LaViSE is evaluated across various domains including its ability to accurately describe a network's internal workings, by consistently ranking importance similar to that reported by human evaluators, and also outperforms previous visualization methods in a visual recognition survey. The frameworks for both implementing and using LaViSE are made publicly available for others to use.

Developing a simplified microscopic model of cuprates is crucial in uncovering the mechanism behind superconductivity, especially due to its strong interactions and complex structural elements. Focusing on one-dimensional models can yield significant insights, as they allow for the long-range nature of electron-phonon interactions that drive superconductivity. We investigate a one-dimensional cuprate system and demonstrate that it exhibits a charged lattice structure, resulting in an unusual long-range electron-phonon interaction. Using molecular beam epitaxy, researchers can grow high-quality, one-dimensional cuprate films on silver substrates, which are then subjected to in-plane mechanical strain. This strain causes a significant shift in the one-dimensional cuprate system's electronic state, as evidenced by point contact spectroscopy experiments that show temperature-dependent gap formation.

The ongoing Population-based HIV Impact Assessment project aims to measure national and regional progress in combating the HIV epidemic, a primary goal of UNAIDS' 90-90-90 targets. By analyzing data from high-risk countries in sub-Saharan Africa, researchers hope to gain a deeper understanding of the key factors driving the epidemic. This study proposes a novel causal learning approach to identify crucial indicators and key indicators driving the outcomes measured by the MHIA survey. This method generates a set of potential causal relationships and a set of key indicators associated with each outcome. The results of the causal learning approach were compared to those from a traditional structural learning algorithm, revealing notable differences in the indicators they identified. Generally, both approaches produced a broad set of indicators, however the causal learning approach produced indicators at a more detailed level. The indicators produced by the causal learning approach are generally correlated with the data but the structural learning approach produced indicators with less confidence. In the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ of $\beta$-Mn type, it's discovered that the transition from a metastable skyrmion lattice at room temperature to an equilibrium helical state, when triggered by magnetic fields along the binary axis, undergoes a first-order phase transition for fields exceeding 6 kOe. Utilizing small-angle neutron scattering, the skyrmion lattice density was found to be directly proportional to the applied magnetic field up to 8 kOe in descending fields, indicating a linear dependence on the magnetic field. Furthermore, neutron diffraction and finite element method simulations while decreasing fields confirmed the presence of topological melting of the skyrmion lattice, where the lattice enters a state of isolated skyrmions before transitioning to "skyrmion gas." The theoretical understanding of the observed topological phase transitions is based on the previously proposed $\beta$-Mn skyrmion stabilization mechanism.
